These problems revolve around education, your actual potential is not the same as what you know.

One thing worth noting is that the "IQ test" as it became known, was never intended to be more than a rough approximate measurement of intellectual capacity.

The predecessor of the IQ test was created by Alfred Binet near the end of the 1800's. At the time is was common for children who failed at school to be labeled as 'stupid' or 'dull', and they were generally assigned to simple classes befitting their limited intellect. (Essentially the education system gave up on them).

The original intention of Binet's test was to find out whether these children who were failing were actually dumb, or if they could be helped with remedial classes. To put it in modern terms, the purpose of the test was to tell the difference between children with learning difficulties (like ADHD or Dyslexia), and those children who were intellectually handicapped. It may seem strange to us now, but at the time they had no effective, impartial way of telling the difference, all they knew was that "Johnny has problems learning to read".

The original IQ test didn't give a score, it was pass/fail. If you passed you were normal, if you failed you were retarded. (literally).

The test didn't have any knowledge requirements, since it was deliberately designed for children who had failed at school, and therefore had a very limited education.

It was only when the test was brought to America, and people realised there was a score, that they started competing and comparing scores.

The test was never designed to with the intention that it would show someone with 125 is smarter than someone who scores 115.. The only thing the test was ever meant say was that someone who scores 100 is normal, someone who scores 115 is normal, someone who scores 125 is normal, and someone who scores 80 or lower is retarded.
